nodes.title: Integral perfectoid, semiperfectoid, quasisyntomic and quasiregular semiperfectoid rings
nodes.statement: (BMS2 4.18) A ring R is perfectoid if it is p-adically complete, there is π ∈ R with π^p = pu for a unit u, Frobenius is surjective on R/p, and ker(θ: A_inf(R) = W(R♭) → R) is principal; then ker θ is generated by a nonzerodivisor ξ = p + [π♭]^p α, L_{R/Z_p} has p-complete Tor-amplitude in degree −1 with p-completion R[1], and R[p^∞] = R[p]. (BMS2 4.10) A is quasisyntomic if p-complete with bounded p^∞-torsion and L_{A/Z_p} has p-complete Tor-amplitude in [−1, 0]; a map of such rings is a quasisyntomic cover if p-completely faithfully flat with p-complete Tor-amplitude of L_{B/A} in [−1, 0]. (BS22 7.1) S is semiperfectoid if it is a derived p-complete ring admitting a surjection from a perfectoid ring; it is quasiregular if in addition it has bounded p^∞-torsion and L_{S/Z_p}[−1] is p-completely flat over S, in which case S is classically p-complete. (BMS2 4.20, 4.22; the identification with BS22 Notation 7.1 is a packet-authored reconciliation via Remarks 4.21-4.22) S is quasiregular semiperfectoid iff quasisyntomic, receiving a map from a perfectoid ring, with S/p semiperfect; conditions (2)-(3) may be replaced by the existence of a surjection from a perfectoid ring.
hypotheses: All completions are p-adic (BMS2) or derived p-adic (BS22 Notation 7.1); BS22 asks only derived p-completeness for semiperfectoid, and Notation 7.1 records that quasiregularity forces classical p-completeness.
Perfectoid here is the integral notion of BMS1 §3, not the Tate-ring notion of PerfectoidSpaces:P1; the comparison for R^+ inside a perfectoid Tate ring is not proved in the sources read (gap).
proofSteps: BMS2 Remark 4.21: semiperfectness of S/p gives Ω¹_{(S/p)/F_p} = 0, so L_{S/R} ⊗^L S/p ∈ D^{≤ −1} for any R → S. For S ∈ QSyn, whose L_{S/Z_p} has p-complete Tor-amplitude in [−1, 0], this places the Tor-amplitude in degree −1.

BMS2 Remark 4.22: given R → S with R perfectoid and S/p semiperfect, R ⊗̂_{Z_p} W(S♭) is perfectoid and surjects onto S (S♭ the inverse-limit perfection of S/p), so the two formulations of the definition agree.
acceptance: The ϖ-adic completion of R^+/(I ∩ R^+) for R^+ integral perfectoid is semiperfectoid (Remark 7.5), and R⟨X^{1/p^∞}⟩/(X − f) for perfectoid R is quasiregular semiperfectoid (proof of Prop. 7.10).

A perfectoid ring is quasiregular semiperfectoid with L_{R/Z_p}^∧ = R[1] (Example 4.24, Proposition 4.19). O_C/p is quasiregular semiperfectoid, and a test must not classify it otherwise. It is p-complete with bounded p-torsion, a quotient of the perfectoid O_C by the nonzerodivisor p, and L_{(O_C/p)/O_C} ≅ (p)/(p²)[1] is p-completely flat in degree −1, so BMS2 Lemma 4.25 applies (the regular-quotient formula is DD.0 content).

sources.excerpt: Fix a semiperfectoid ring S, i.e. S is a derived p-complete ring that can be written as a quotient of a perfectoid ring R. We recall that S is called quasiregular if S has bounded p^∞-torsion, and the cotangent complex L_{S/Z_p}[−1] is p-completely flat over S

sources.excerpt: A ring S is quasiregular semiperfectoid if: (1) The ring S is quasisyntomic, i.e. S ∈ QSyn. (2) There exists a map R → S with R perfectoid. (3) The Frobenius of S/pS is surjective, i.e. S/pS is semiperfect.

nodes.title: Maps out of a perfect prism are determined by their reduction: (A_inf(R), ker θ) is initial in (R)_Δ
nodes.statement: Let (A, I) be a perfect prism with perfectoid ring R = A/I. For any prism (B, J), any ring map A/I → B/J lifts uniquely to a map of prisms (A, I) → (B, J). Hence (R)_Δ = (R/A)_Δ. The dual statement fails: a prism (A, I) may admit several maps to a perfect prism (B, J) with the same reduction.
hypotheses: (A, I) perfect (φ_A bijective); B and B/J derived p-complete; B may have p-torsion, which is why being a δ-map must be checked separately.

Uses that L_{A/Z_p} vanishes after derived p-completion because A is the ring of Witt vectors of a perfect F_p-algebra. The source states this without proof; identifying a perfect prism with W(A/p) is Corollary 2.31, a packet-supplied reference.

Placement: Lemma 4.8 is an application of PR.0's perfect-prism/perfectoid-ring correspondence and rigidity, so it is filed under Q0:animated-application (which imports PR.0), not under Q0:integral-algebra (which PR.0 itself requires).
proofSteps: Deformation theory: Hom(A, B) ≅ Hom(A, B/J) ≅ Hom(A, B/(J, p)) since L_{A/Z_p}^∧ = 0 and B, B/J are derived p-complete; so A → A/I → B/J lifts uniquely to α: A → B, compatible with Frobenius lifts, with α(I) ⊂ J.

α is a δ-map: it factors uniquely through B^perf = lim_φ B → B by bijectivity of φ on A; B^perf is a perfect δ-ring, hence p-torsionfree, so the φ-equivariant map A → B^perf is automatically a δ-map, and B^perf → B is a δ-map by construction.

The proof ends there: α is a δ-map with α(I) ⊂ J, hence a map of prisms. Rigidity (Lemma 3.5, IB = J) is not used in Lemma 4.8. It is used in the proof of Proposition 7.2 ("K = dC by Lemma 3.5"), and the PR.0 rigidity link was re-targeted there by REVIEW-EXT-03.
acceptance: For R = O_C and any prism (B, J) with a map O_C → B/J, there is a unique prism map (A_inf(O_C), (ξ)) → (B, J), so the absolute prismatic site of Spf O_C is the relative site over A_inf.
The uniqueness fails for maps into perfect prisms from non-perfect prisms (remark after Lemma 4.8).

sources.locator: Section 4.1, Remark 4.7 and Lemma 4.8 with proof, pp. 38-39 (extraction lines 1736-1758)
sources.excerpt: To check α is a δ-map, note that α factors uniquely over B^perf := lim_φ B → B by the bijectivity of φ on A. As B^perf is a perfect δ-ring, it is p-torsionfree. Thus, the φ-equivariant map A → B^perf is automatically a δ-map.
sources.match: The p-torsion subtlety in the proof that the lift is a map of prisms.

nodes.title: The category of prisms under a semiperfectoid ring has an initial object with principal ideal
nodes.statement: For a semiperfectoid ring S, the category of all prisms (A, I) with a map S → A/I has an initial object (Δ^init_S, I) with I = (d) principal. Δ^init_S is a derived (p, d)-complete δ-A_inf(R)-algebra in which d is a nonzerodivisor, obtained from B = A_inf(R){x_f | f ∈ J}/(d x_f − f | f ∈ J)_δ (J = ker(A_inf(R) → R → S)) by killing the smallest δ-stable ideal containing the d^∞-torsion, taking H^0 of the derived (p, d)-completion, and iterating transfinitely. The source identifies this category with the absolute prismatic site (Spf S)_Δ of Remark 4.7. The objects of that site are bounded prisms, whereas Δ^init_S "is not bounded in general", so Δ^init_S need not be an object of (Spf S)_Δ.
hypotheses: S = R/J' for a perfectoid ring R (surjection chosen); (A_inf(R), ker θ = (d)) is the initial prism under R (Lemma 4.8) and ker θ is principal.
Δ^init_S is not bounded in general; its perfection is the well-behaved object (Corollary 7.3).
The transfinite induction uses that derived completion commutes with ω₁-filtered colimits.

Asserted, not argued: that the transfinite torsion-removal process ends in a d-torsion-free derived (p, d)-complete ring still receiving a unique map to every (C, K), and that Remark 4.7's bounded site is the category meant.
proofSteps: Given a prism (C, K) with S → C/K, Lemma 4.8 gives a unique (A_inf(R), (d)) → (C, K) and K = dC by rigidity (Lemma 3.5); d is a nonzerodivisor in C, so each f ∈ J has a unique quotient f/d ∈ C.

Freely adjoining x_f with d x_f = f in δ-rings gives a unique δ-map B → C; since C is d-torsionfree it factors through B/B[d^∞]_δ, and since C is derived (p, d)-complete and classical, through H^0 of the derived (p, d)-completion.

The completed quotient may acquire new d-torsion; transfinite iteration (completion commuting with ω₁-filtered colimits) produces Δ^init_S with d a nonzerodivisor and still a unique map to (C, K); d is distinguished, so (Δ^init_S, (d)) is a prism.
R = A_inf(R)/d → Δ^init_S/d factors through S because all elements of J become divisible by d.
acceptance: For S = R perfectoid, Δ^init_S = A_inf(R) by Lemma 4.8, since (A_inf(R), ker θ) is already initial among prisms under R.
For S = R/(f) with f admitting compatible p-power roots, Corollary 7.3 and the proof of Theorem 7.4 together give that the p-adic completion of (Δ^init_S)_perf/I is the p-completion of R/(f^{1/p^∞}).

sources.locator: Section 7.1, Proposition 7.2 with proof, p. 55 (extraction lines 2426-2461)
sources.excerpt: The latter δ-ring may however contain new d-torsion elements; but after a transfinite induction (using that completion commutes with ω₁-filtered colimits), we arrive at a derived (p, d)-complete δ-A_inf(R)-algebra Δ^init_S such that d is a nonzerodivisor.
sources.match: The torsion-removal and completion loop that the stage text calls 'the explicit adjoining, torsion-removal and transfinite completion argument of 7.2'.

nodes.title: Universal perfectoid ring S_perfd under a semiperfectoid ring
nodes.statement: For semiperfectoid S there is a universal perfectoid ring S_perfd with a map S → S_perfd (every map from S to a perfectoid ring factors uniquely through it), namely S_perfd = p-adic completion of (Δ^init_S)_perf / I, where (Δ^init_S)_perf is the completed perfection of the initial prism.
hypotheses: Uses the equivalence between perfectoid rings and perfect prisms (Theorem 3.10; supplied by PrismaticCohomology:PR.0/perfect-prisms-perfectoid-rings) so that perfectoid rings under S are perfect prisms under (Δ^init_S, I).

Uses Lemma 3.9: the completed perfection (A_∞, IA_∞) of a prism is the universal perfect prism under it, IA_perf = (d) with d, p nonzerodivisors and A_perf/d[p^∞] = A_perf/d[p]; the derived and classical (p, I)-completions agree.
proofSteps: Perfectoid rings S_perfd with S → S_perfd correspond to perfect prisms (A, I) with R → A/I factoring through S, i.e. to perfect prisms under (Δ^init_S, I).
Lemma 3.9 identifies the universal perfect prism under (Δ^init_S, I) as its completed perfection; reduce modulo I and note the quotient is p-adically complete (bounded p-torsion).
acceptance: For S perfectoid, S_perfd = S.
Theorem 7.4 asserts S → S_perfd is surjective; before that theorem only the universal property is known.

sources.locator: Section 7.1, Corollary 7.3 with proof, p. 56 (extraction lines 2463-2468), and Lemma 3.9 with proof, pp. 31-32 (extraction lines 1434-1448)
sources.excerpt: Note that the category of perfectoid rings S_perfd with a map S → S_perfd is equivalent to the category of perfect prisms (A, I) with a map R → A/I. Thus, the claim follows from Lemma 3.9.
sources.match: The two-line proof and its two imports (Theorem 3.10 and Lemma 3.9).

nodes.title: Derived prismatic cohomology by left Kan extension, with its Hodge-Tate filtration and formal properties
nodes.statement: For a bounded prism (A, I), the functor R ↦ Δ_{R/A} on p-completely smooth A/I-algebras (valued in commutative algebras in (p, I)-complete objects of D(A) with φ_A-semilinear Frobenius) is left Kan extended to all derived p-complete simplicial commutative A/I-algebras. The Hodge-Tate comparison (Theorem 6.3) yields on Δ̄_{R/A} := Δ_{R/A} ⊗^L_A A/I an exhaustive increasing N-indexed filtration with gr^i = derived p-completion of ∧^i L_{R/(A/I)}{−i}[−i]. Consequences: (1) agreement with Δ_{R/A} for p-completely smooth R; (2) R ↦ Δ_{R/A} is a sheaf for the p-completely etale topology; (3) for perfect (A, I) it is a quasisyntomic sheaf on quasisyntomic A/I-algebras; (4) base change Δ_{R_B/B} ≅ Δ_{R/A} ⊗̂^L_A B for maps of bounded prisms (A, I) → (B, J), R_B the derived p-completion of R ⊗^L_A B; (5) the functor is symmetric monoidal and commutes with all colimits.
hypotheses: (A, I) bounded; left Kan extension in the sense of Lurie HTT §5.5.9 along the inclusion of p-completely smooth algebras into derived p-complete simplicial commutative A/I-algebras.

This construction is owned by PrismaticCohomology:PR.2 according to stage Q2 ('Import PR.2's independent extension'); no PR.2 node exists yet in the PrismaticCohomology draft, so the construction is recorded here as read (see gap).
Properties (2)-(5) are asserted as 'immediate consequences' of the Hodge-Tate filtration; the source gives no further argument.
proofSteps: Define Δ_{R/A} as the left Kan extension; on smooth algebras nothing changes (1).

The Hodge-Tate comparison for smooth algebras (Theorem 6.3: Ω^i_{R/(A/I)} ≅ H^i(Δ̄_{R/A}){i}) left-Kan-extends to the filtration with graded pieces the completed derived exterior powers of the cotangent complex, since ∧^i L extends Ω^i.

(2)-(5) are stated as "immediate consequences". Packet-authored reading: they follow from the filtration by etale/quasisyntomic descent of completed derived exterior powers of the cotangent complex, base change of L, and colimit preservation of the associated graded. For (3) the source points only to a variant for derived de Rham cohomology in characteristic p ([BMS19, Example 5.11], unread).
acceptance: For R = A/I⟨X⟩, gr^1 = R{−1}[−1] and the filtration recovers the Hodge-Tate comparison Ω¹ ≅ H¹(Δ̄){1}.
For R with L_{R/(A/I)}[−1] p-completely flat (e.g. quasiregular semiperfectoid over a perfect prism) all gr^i are discrete, so Δ̄_{R/A} is discrete (used in 7.10).

sources.locator: Section 7.2, Construction 7.6 and consequences (1)-(5), pp. 56-57 (extraction lines 2494-2532); Theorem 6.3 statement, p. 52 (extraction lines 2353-2356)
sources.excerpt: The Hodge-Tate comparison shows that Δ̄_{R/A} := Δ_{R/A} ⊗^L_A A/I admits an exhaustive increasing N-indexed filtration with gr^i given by sending R to the derived p-completion of ∧^i L_{R/(A/I)}{−i}[−i]
sources.match: The filtered Hodge-Tate comparison for derived prismatic cohomology required by stage Q2.

nodes.title: When Δ_{R/A} is discrete it is a δ-ring, a prism over (A, I), and weakly initial with an idempotent retract that is initial
nodes.statement: Let (A, I) be a bounded prism and R a derived p-complete simplicial A/I-algebra with Δ_{R/A} concentrated in degree 0. Then (1) the φ_A-linear Frobenius on Δ_{R/A} lifts naturally to a δ-A-structure; (2) (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is a prism over (A, I) with a map R → Δ̄_{R/A}; (3) the category of prisms (B, J) over (A, I) with R → B/J has an initial object, (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is weakly initial, and the initial object is the retract of an idempotent endomorphism of (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}). (Lemma 7.8) In an idempotent complete category C, if the identity factors through C_{X\} → C via F: C → C_{X\}, then F(X) is an idempotent of X whose retract is initial in C.
hypotheses: Discreteness of Δ_{R/A} (hence of Δ̄_{R/A} = Δ_{R/A} ⊗^L_A A/I for (2)).

The δ-structure is obtained from the functorial Čech-Alexander model F_A(R) and the map F_A(R) → W_2(F_A(R)) classifying δ-structures, together with the pullback square W_2(B) = B ×_{B ⊗^L F_p} B for simplicial commutative rings.
BS22 conjectures that (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is itself initial; only weak initiality plus the retract is proved.

Lemma 7.8 is stated for an idempotent complete category. The source applies it to (R/A)_Δ without checking idempotent completeness; this is a gap. In part (3), "Using the argument from part (1), one shows that this is in fact a map of δ-rings" is asserted.
proofSteps: (1) Build the map Δ_{R/A} ≅ colim lim F_A(R) → colim lim W_2(F_A(R)) of E_∞-rings over A → W_2(A), splitting restriction; identify the target with W_2(Δ_{R/A}) using the pullback square and discreteness; this is a δ-structure refining φ_R.
(2) Immediate from derived (p, I)-completeness and discreteness of Δ̄_{R/A}.

(3) For any (B, J) in (R/A)_Δ, resolving R by p-completely ind-smooth R_i and writing Δ_{R/A} = colim_{Δ^op} lim_{C ∈ (R_•/A)_Δ} C, restrict the limit to the compatible objects defined by (B, J) to get a functorial δ-map Δ_{R/A} → B; conclude by Lemma 7.8 (faithful F, epimorphism X → X', at most one and at least one map X' → Y).
acceptance: Lemma 7.8 applied to C = (R/A)_Δ with X = (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) gives the initial object as a retract.
In Example 7.9 and Proposition 7.10 the idempotent is shown to be the identity.

sources.locator: Section 7.2, Lemma 7.7 with proof and Lemma 7.8 with proof, pp. 57-59 (extraction lines 2533-2617)
sources.excerpt: In particular, the initial object is the image of some idempotent endomorphism of (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}). In part (3), we conjecture that (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is actually the initial object.

nodes.title: For a Koszul-regular quotient R = A/(I, f_1, ..., f_r) with bounded p-torsion, Δ_{R/A} is the prismatic envelope and initial
nodes.statement: Fix a bounded prism (A, I) and R = A/J with J = (I, f_1, ..., f_r), f_1, ..., f_r Koszul-regular on A/I, R with bounded p-torsion. Then Δ_{R/A} is concentrated in degree 0 and I-torsionfree, and (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is the initial object of (R/A)_Δ; locally where I = (d), Δ_{R/A} = A{f_1/d, ..., f_r/d}^∧ (the prismatic envelope A{J/I}^∧ of Proposition 3.13).
hypotheses: Koszul-regularity of f_1, ..., f_r on A/I and bounded p-torsion of R; principal I after localization on Spf A.

Imports: Proposition 3.13 (prismatic envelopes of regular ideals; supplied by PrismaticCohomology:PR.0/regular-prismatic-envelopes), Lemma 7.7, the Hodge-Tate filtration, and a standard free-resolution computation cited to [Bha12, Claim 3.30] (unread).

Also used: Lemma 7.7(1)-(2) to regard (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) as an object of (R/A)_Δ, and the assertion "the formation of both sides commutes with arbitrary base change" (Construction 7.6(4) for Δ, free δ-adjunction for B).
proofSteps: Δ_{R/A} is discrete and I-torsionfree by the Hodge-Tate filtration (gr^i are completed exterior powers of L_{R/(A/I)} = J/(J² + I)[1]), so it is an object of (R/A)_Δ.

Base change reduces the comparison B := A{f_i/d}^∧ → Δ_{R/A} to the universal case A = Z_p{d, f_1, ..., f_r}[δ(d)^{-1}]^∧, where A/I and R are p-torsionfree and f_1, ..., f_r is p-completely regular relative to A_0/I_0 for (A_0, I_0) = (Z_p{d}[δ(d)^{-1}]^∧, (d)); Proposition 3.13 identifies B with the prismatic envelope, discrete and initial in (R/A)_Δ.

B → Δ_{R/A} has a retraction by Lemma 7.7, so B/IB → Δ̄_{R/A} has p-torsionfree cokernel; it suffices that B/IB[1/p] → Δ̄_{R/A}[1/p] is surjective, which holds because Δ̄_{R/A}[1/p] is generated as a Banach R[1/p]-algebra by gr^1 = J/(J² + I){−1} and J/I maps onto it.
acceptance: R = A/(I, f) with f a nonzerodivisor on A/I and R of bounded p-torsion: Δ_{R/A} = A{f/d}^∧, and the initial prism is obtained by adjoining f/d.
The example is the engine of Proposition 7.10 via the rings T = R⟨X_1^{1/p^∞}, ..., X_r^{1/p^∞}⟩/(X_1 − f_1, ..., X_r − f_r).

sources.locator: Section 7.2, Example 7.9 with proof, p. 59 (extraction lines 2618-2644)
sources.excerpt: By the construction of the prismatic envelope in Proposition 3.13, it follows that B identifies with the prismatic envelope A{J/I}^∧; this implies that B is concentrated in degree 0 and (B, IB) is the initial object of (R/A)_Δ.
sources.match: The point where PR.0's envelope construction enters the semiperfectoid theory.

nodes.title: For quasiregular semiperfectoid S, Δ_{S/A} is discrete, equals the initial prism Δ^init_S independently of the perfectoid R, and S → Δ̄_S is p-completely faithfully flat
nodes.statement: Let S be quasiregular semiperfectoid, R → S any map from a perfectoid ring, (A, I) = (A_inf(R), ker θ). Then Δ_{S/A} is discrete, (Δ_{S/A}, IΔ_{S/A}) is the initial prism Δ^init_S with a map S → Δ^init_S/I (so Δ_{S/A} does not depend on R), and S → Δ̄_{S/A} = Δ_{S/A}/I is p-completely faithfully flat. Notation: Δ_S := Δ^init_S = Δ_{S/A}.

nodes.title: Andre's flatness lemma: every perfectoid ring has a p-completely faithfully flat absolutely integrally closed perfectoid extension
nodes.statement: Let R be a perfectoid ring. There is a p-completely faithfully flat map R → S of perfectoid rings with S absolutely integrally closed (every monic polynomial over S has a root); in particular every element of S admits a compatible system of p-power roots. The map can moreover be chosen to be an ind-syntomic cover modulo p (Remark 7.15, sketched).

(Proposition 7.11(2) gives flatness of (A, I) → (B, IB)_perf; the proof of Theorem 7.14 writes "perfect prism (B, IB)" for this perfection.)
Transfinitely iterate R ↦ R_1 to obtain a quasisyntomic cover R → R' with R' perfectoid and absolutely integrally closed.

Remark 7.15 (sketch): for S = R⟨Y^{1/p^∞}⟩/(f(Y)), the map S → Δ̄_S is a cover (Prop. 7.10); after reducing to p-torsionfree R and choosing ϖ with (ϖ^p) = (p), φ_A^*(T/ϖ) is the pd-envelope of f(Y) in R/ϖ[Y^{1/p^∞}] (Corollary 2.39), and pd-envelopes of nonzerodivisors in F_p-algebras are ind-syntomic (A/f^p[g_1, g_2, ...]/(g_i^p)), lifting along nilpotent thickenings; alternatively [GR, Theorem 16.9.17].

nodes.statement: For any semiperfectoid ring S, the map S → S_perfd to the universal perfectoid ring under S is surjective. In the principal case S = R/(f) with R perfectoid and f admitting compatible p-power roots, S_perfd is the p-adic completion of R/(f^{1/p^∞}).

nodes.title: Closed perfectoid quotients: the vanishing locus of an ideal in an affinoid perfectoid space is strongly Zariski closed
nodes.statement: Let X = Spa(R, R^+) be affinoid perfectoid (R a perfectoid Tate ring with pseudo-uniformizer ϖ, R^+ ⊂ R° open and integrally closed) and I ⊂ R an ideal. Let S be the ϖ-adic completion of R^+/(I ∩ R^+); S is semiperfectoid, R' := S_perfd[1/ϖ] is a perfectoid Tate ring which is a quotient of R, every map from R to a perfectoid ring vanishing on I factors uniquely through R', and the vanishing locus of I in X is the strongly Zariski closed subset Spa(R', R'^+) with R'^+ the minimal open integrally closed subring of R' containing the image of R^+. Hence (ECD 5.8) every Zariski closed immersion Z → X (closed immersion whose image is the zero locus of an ideal) is strongly Zariski closed (Z = Spa(S, S^+) affinoid with R → S surjective and S^+ the integral closure of R^+ in S); the claim in [Sch15, Remark II.2.4] that the notions differ was erroneous. ECD adds that Theorem 7.4 also implies almost surjectivity on plus rings, independently of [KL15, 3.6.9(c)].
hypotheses: S must be semiperfectoid. BS22 asserts "S is a semiperfectoid ring" without proof. The required input is BMS1 Lemma 3.20, read by the reviewer: if a complete Tate ring R is perfectoid in Fontaine's sense, then every ring of integral elements R^+ is an integral perfectoid ring. Sch12 perfectoid K-algebras are perfectoid in Fontaine's sense (remark after 3.20). S is then a quotient of R^+ and derived p-complete. The proof of 3.20 imports BMS1 Lemmas 3.9-3.10 and [45, Lemma 5.5], none read.

Passing between S_perfd (integral, p-complete) and R' (Tate) needs the ϖ-adic and p-adic topologies on R^+ to agree. This holds when p is a unit of R, since p is then a pseudo-uniformizer; ϖ^p | p alone does not give it. In characteristic p, derived p-completeness is automatic and the ϖ-adic completion of Remark 7.5 must be used. The source does not discuss either case.

ECD's printed remark reads 'S^+ → R^+ is almost surjective'; the mathematically meaningful direction is R^+ → S^+ (almost surjectivity of the plus ring map), as in [KL15, 3.6.9(c)]; recorded as a probable misprint.
proofSteps: Form S = (R^+/(I ∩ R^+))^∧_ϖ; by Theorem 7.4, S → S_perfd is surjective, so R^+ → S_perfd is surjective and R → R' = S_perfd[1/ϖ] is surjective.

Universal property: a continuous map R → T to a perfectoid Tate ring vanishing on I sends R^+ into T° and vanishes on I ∩ R^+, hence induces S → T°. T° is an integral perfectoid ring by BMS1 Lemma 3.20, so this gives S_perfd → T° and then R' → T, which is unique because R → R' is surjective. The integrality and continuity inputs are packet-authored; the source says only "any map from R to a perfectoid ring that vanishes on I factors uniquely over R'".

The vanishing locus of I is therefore Spa(R', R'^+) with R'^+ the minimal open integrally closed subring containing the image of R^+; this is strongly Zariski closed by definition, giving ECD Theorem 5.8 via Definition 5.7.
acceptance: For X = Spa(K⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩, K°⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩) and I = (T): S = (K°⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩/(T))^∧ and, by the principal case of Theorem 7.4 (T has compatible roots), S_perfd = K°, so R' = K. The Zariski closed subset is the origin Spa(K, K°), and the kernel of R → R' is the closed ideal generated by all T^{1/p^n}, not (T).

Diagonals (for affinoid X = Spa(R, R^+), Y = Spa(S, S^+)): Δ_f is strongly Zariski closed because S ⊗̂_R S → S is surjective, so Δ_f is an immersion (ECD Proposition 5.9). This uses only the definitions, not Theorem 5.8.
